pages.x: In June 793 raiders from the sea fell on the monastery of Lindisfarne, an island off northeast England. They killed monks and carried off treasure and young men as slaves. The scholar Alcuin wrote that such terror had never been seen in Britain before. The Viking Age had begun.
The Vikings' secret was the longship: long, light and shallow, with a sail and oars, able to cross the open sea and row far up rivers.
pages.fx: They could strike almost anywhere without warning and be gone before an army arrived. Rich, unguarded monasteries were easy prey.

pages.x: Raids grew into invasions. In 845 Vikings rowed up the Seine, and the Frankish king paid them 7,000 pounds of silver to leave Paris. In 865 a great Danish army landed in England and conquered every English kingdom but one, Wessex.

In 878 a surprise attack drove King Alfred of Wessex into the marshes of Somerset, where, legend says, he let a peasant woman's cakes burn. Months later he beat the Danes at Edington. England was split: the Danes kept the north and east, and Alfred's heirs went on to unite the rest.

In 911 the Frankish king gave a Viking chief, Rollo, land at the mouth of the Seine if he would keep other Vikings out. It became Normandy, the land of the Northmen. A story says Rollo would not kiss the king's foot, and the man he told to do it lifted the foot so high that the king fell over.

Swedish Vikings went east, down the rivers of Russia to the Black Sea and the Caspian, trading furs and slaves for Arab silver. They were called the Rus, and gave their name to the state of Kyiv and to Russia. In Constantinople, Norsemen served as the emperor's Varangian Guard.

Westward, Norse settlers reached Iceland around 870 and Greenland in 985. Around 1000 Leif Erikson sailed on to a land he called Vinland. At the tip of Newfoundland archaeologists found their houses, the first Europeans in America, five centuries before Columbus.

The Viking Age is often said to end in 1066, when Harald Hardrada, king of Norway and once a captain of the Varangian Guard, invaded England and was killed at Stamford Bridge. Weeks later Normans, descendants of Rollo, landed in the south.

The Vikings were raiders, but also traders, farmers, poets and explorers. They built up towns such as Dublin and York, founded Normandy, settled Iceland, where their sagas were written, and left English words such as sky, egg, knife and window.
